cells.tense: You're in the middle of it right now, hands in the work, tending something that's coming along, and you're keeping two demands level without letting either one drown the other.
cells.ask: Let one thing finish in front of someone who'll see it done
cells.core:
What this looks like when it's working: you give the thing what it needs — light, water, time — and then you step back and let it do its own growing. You're not forcing it and you're not hovering. You keep two demands fed at once, and neither one sits waiting at the edge of the table.

That steadiness is why the thing you're growing feels safe enough to actually grow. When something here reaches its end, let it be an end. Say the work is finished and take the acknowledgment that comes with it, because you don't have to keep one hand on it after it's done. Honor's act belongs here: a release that feels like fulfillment and not like defeat, available today, at the finished edge of this.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping two things alive at once, and neither one feels left behind.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the part of your life where something is still small and needs looking after

cells.tense: You're living in how this turns out, sorting out what it'll need before it's shown you, and the tending has run out ahead of the thing itself.
cells.ask: Set down one future you're holding open and let today's version be enough
cells.core:
In good shape, this is care that doesn't exhaust — you give what's needed and then you let the thing grow on its own, holding space without clutching. You make conditions and then get out of the way. That's the shape of it when it's right.

What's happening now is you're managing outcomes that haven't arrived, paying for work that may not be yours, deciding what will be needed before the need shows up. From inside it feels like care. From outside it's exhausting, and it's costing the ease care was supposed to have. Dream forward out of what you've actually lived through instead of out of what might go wrong — real satisfaction grows out of experience you've already digested, and it shows up on its own once you've stopped bracing for it.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending the version that hasn't arrived, and it's wearing you out.

cells.tense: You used to be the one in the middle of it — hands in the soil — and you're standing past that door now, watching from a distance instead of reaching in.
cells.ask: Pick up one small piece of the tending today, just the next inch, and do that
cells.core:
This is care that doesn't clutch: you set the conditions and then stay clear of the way, and that's exactly what lets something grow on its own terms. You know how to be present without hovering. You know how to hold room for something without needing to steer it.

The reaching-in has stopped here. Nothing's growing because nobody's watering it — the tending and the one it was for have both gone quiet. You can't force the feeling back; pressing on a starved thing doesn't feed it. The pull comes from still hoping for it, still following through on it, and that wanting is what brings your hands back to the soil. Take the next inch today, not the whole row.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reaching in, and the tending went quiet with you.

cells.tense: You're already shaping how this develops — the pace, what it needs, when to wait — and you speak about it as though it were simply happening to you.
cells.ask: Claim one thing you keep alive by choice
cells.core:
Working well, this is care that doesn't exhaust: you give what's needed and then let the thing find its own way. Nothing forced, nothing held too tight — just the patient attention that lets something come up. That's what you actually do here, most of the time, without noting it as anything.

The noticing is what's missing. The tending is real and it's yours, and you've been filing it under what the job needed or what someone else was owed. Pick one thing you keep alive by your own choosing, say out loud that it's yours, and let it be honored — starting with you. What you've been calling simply necessary is a choice you're already making.
cells.sheetLine: The tending is yours. You've been calling it someone else's need.
